title: Reaching a machine without SSH

story: Sean approved the plan for RH-1234, and the orchestrator, the service that runs every agent's workflow, has just claimed a full VM for the build. Now it must start Nova's harness on that machine. The VM has no SSH key, no open port and no public address, and its security group accepts no incoming connection at all. There is no door to knock on.

And whatever starts the harness must not stop it. The build may take an hour, and then Nova may ask Sean a question and wait for the answer until tomorrow. Nobody can say in advance how long the work will run.
hook.question: How do you start a program on a machine that accepts no connections, and keep it running for as long as the work takes?

read.h: The machine calls out for its work
p: Every sandbox VM runs the SSM agent, a small program from AWS Systems Manager that runs as root. Instead of waiting for someone to connect, it connects out to Systems Manager, through the interface endpoints from the network lesson, and keeps asking whether there is work for this machine. That is why nothing needs to connect in. You can think of it as SSH without port 22 and without keys, as long as you remember where the comparison stops: you do not get a live terminal, you send a job and read its result later.

The job is called a command. The orchestrator calls SendCommand with a document, AWS-RunShellScript, and the shell lines to run as its parameters. AWS returns a command ID at once, the agent receives the command a moment later, and each machine's result, called an invocation, moves from Pending to InProgress to Success, Failed or TimedOut, with the output attached. IAM decides on both sides: the VM's role carries the managed policy that lets the agent receive commands, and the orchestrator's role may send AWS-RunShellScript only to instances tagged ai-agents:managed=true.

code.file: what the orchestrator does, written with the AWS CLI
code.text:
aws ssm send-command \
  --instance-ids i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 \
  --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --parameters 'commands=["systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-42 || systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-42 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run /run/nova/task.json"]' \
  --query Command.CommandId --output text

aws ssm get-command-invocation --command-id <the id from above> \
  --instance-id i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 --query Status --output text

notes.text: The document: AWS's ready-made "run these shell lines" job.
The shell line itself. The next sections explain why it looks like this.
Ask for the result on this one machine: Pending, InProgress, then Success, Failed or TimedOut.

read.h: A command has a deadline, and a run has none
p: An SSM command is not meant to live for long. AWS-RunShellScript has an executionTimeout that is one hour by default and 48 hours at most, and when that time is over, SSM stops the command and everything it started. A Nova run cannot live inside that, because the platform deliberately puts no time limit on runs: a run may wait days for a person, and cutting it in the middle destroys work. A tool's built-in timeout is still a time limit, even if nobody chose it on purpose.
So the command must not be the work. It should start the work, hand it to something that keeps it alive, and end in about a second. On Linux, that something is systemd.

read.h: systemd keeps the long job alive
p: systemd is the program that starts and watches every service on a Linux machine. If you have used pm2 to keep a Node server running, it is the same job, done by the operating system itself. Each thing systemd manages is a unit, and a service unit runs one program: systemd starts it, keeps its logs in the journal, and knows at any moment whether it is active, inactive or failed. Usually units are files written in advance, but systemd-run creates one on the spot, a transient unit, and returns at once while the program keeps running.

So the command that the orchestrator sends is one line. It asks systemd whether the unit for this run, nova-run-42, is already active, and only if it is not, starts the harness in that unit as the agent user. The check matters because of retries. The orchestrator runs on Temporal, a workflow engine that saves every step, and each step that talks to the outside world (an activity) is retried when the worker process running it dies. The retry sends the same command again. With the check, the second command finds the harness running and does nothing, so the retry simply joins the work that is already happening. After that, the orchestrator never asks SSM about the run again. It follows the harness's heartbeats instead: a small "I am still working" message every 30 seconds, sent through the broker, our service that holds the GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials.

code.file: the shell line sent over SSM, and how to look at the unit afterwards
code.text:
# Sent over SSM. The command ends in about a second; the unit keeps running.
systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-42 ||
  systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-42 \
    /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run /run/nova/task.json

# Later, on the VM:
systemctl is-active nova-run-42            # active, inactive or failed
journalctl -u nova-run-42 -o cat -n 3      # the harness's latest log lines
systemctl stop nova-run-42                 # what releasing the VM ends with

notes.text: is-active --quiet only sets the exit code: 0 if the unit runs. || means "only if that failed".
A transient unit named after the run, owned by the user agent, not root.
The harness and its task file. Nothing here tells systemd how long it may run.
-o cat prints only the messages, without dates and host names.

p: Systems Manager keeps a history of every command in the account: the document, the parameters and the output. Anyone allowed to call ssm:ListCommands can read it. The orchestrator writes each run's task, broker capability and gateway token to /run/nova/ on the VM over SSM, so those values appear in that history. The threat model lists this as a known soft spot, and it is accepted because none of these values is a key to an outside service, and they all stop working when the run ends.
Keep it that way: never put a real secret, such as a GitHub token or an API key, into a command. Session Manager, the interactive shell that SSM also offers, is not used for runs.

lab.title: Send a command, then hand the work to systemd
needs: Docker Desktop running (about 200 MB for a small Ubuntu image with systemd)
AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab
lab.goal: Send the start command the SSM way and find it in the account's command history, then use a container with systemd as a pretend VM to see a time-limited command die and a systemd unit live on.

guess.q: You send the harness itself as an SSM command, with executionTimeout set to the maximum, 48 hours. On the second day, Nova asks Sean a question, and he answers three days later. What happens?

options.text: SSM stops the command after 48 hours, and the harness is killed in the middle of its wait.
options.why: The timeout is a hard limit on the command and everything it started. That is why the command only starts a systemd unit.

options.text: SSM extends the timeout because the harness is still busy.
options.why: SSM does not look at what the command is doing. When the time is up, it stops the command.

options.text: Nothing, because the harness runs as the agent user, not as root.
options.why: The user does not matter. Everything the command started is stopped with it.

follow.say: Start LocalStack if it is not running from an earlier lab, point the AWS CLI at it, and create a pretend instance to send commands to.
follow.do:
docker run --rm -d --name localstack -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p3-5 && cd ~/academy-labs/p3-5 && export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-03cf127a --instance-type m8i.xlarge --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text) && echo $ID

follow.say: Send the start command, and ask for its result. LocalStack runs nothing on the pretend instance, so it reports Success with no output; a real VM would run the line.
follow.do:
C=$(aws ssm send-command --instance-ids $ID --document-name AWS-RunShellScript --parameters 'commands=["systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-42 || systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-42 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run /run/nova/task.json"]' --query Command.CommandId --output text) && echo $C
aws ssm get-command-invocation --command-id $C --instance-id $ID --query Status --output text

follow.say: Read the account's command history, because whatever you send is stored there for anyone who may list commands.
follow.see: AWS-RunShellScript	systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-42 || systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-42 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run /run/nova/task.json

follow.say: Build a pretend VM: a container that runs systemd and has an agent user, like the sandbox image. It needs --privileged so systemd can manage processes inside it.
follow.do:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM ubuntu:24.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends systemd systemd-sysv && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN useradd -m -u 1001 agent
CMD ["/sbin/init"]
EOF
docker build -q -t academy-systemd . && docker run -d --name sandbox --privileged --cgroupns=host -v /sys/fs/cgroup:/sys/fs/cgroup:rw academy-systemd && sleep 6 && docker exec sandbox systemctl is-system-running
follow.see:
sha256:5987d084a0418ad2dc7f7c0919fa19799829fdcb05a04241c279871fa2e678b0
280e24e97e9b4f0d8a2c…
running
(degraded is fine too: a few services do not start in a container)

follow.say: Install a pretend harness that works forever and reports every 5 seconds.
follow.do:
cat > nova-worker <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# A pretend harness: works on one run for a long time and reports every 5 seconds.
echo "nova-worker: starting $2 as $(whoami)"
i=0
while true; do
  i=$((i + 1))
  echo "nova-worker: still working on $2 ($i)"
  sleep 5
done
EOF
docker cp nova-worker sandbox:/usr/local/bin/nova-worker && docker exec sandbox chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker

follow.say: First the wrong way: run the harness inside a command with a time limit, the way an SSM command with a 12-second executionTimeout would. docker exec plays the part of the SSM agent here.
follow.do: docker exec sandbox timeout 12 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run run-41; echo "exit $?"
follow.see:
nova-worker: starting run-41 as root
nova-worker: still working on run-41 (1)
nova-worker: still working on run-41 (2)
nova-worker: still working on run-41 (3)
exit 124
(124 means the time limit killed it)

follow.say: Now the right way: the command hands the harness to systemd and returns at once. Wait 15 seconds, longer than the old limit, and look again.
follow.do:
docker exec sandbox systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-42 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run run-42
sleep 15 && docker exec sandbox systemctl is-active nova-run-42
docker exec sandbox journalctl -u nova-run-42 -o cat --no-pager | head -3
follow.see:
Running as unit: nova-run-42.service; invocation ID: 146cb2fbc22d4a4a9e324e33af08c928
active
Started nova-run-42.service - /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run run-42.
nova-worker: starting run-42 as agent
nova-worker: still working on run-42 (1)

lab.build: Temporal retries the start activity when an orchestrator worker dies, so the start command must be safe to send twice. Write the check-then-start line for run-43 (systemctl is-active --quiet ... || systemd-run ...) and send it to the pretend VM twice with docker exec sandbox sh -c '<your line>'; echo "exit $?". Both must exit 0. Then prove there is exactly one unit for run-43 with docker exec sandbox systemctl list-units 'nova-*' --no-pager, and end the run the way releasing a VM does: systemctl stop nova-run-43, then is-active must print inactive.
checks: get-command-invocation prints Success, and list-commands shows the full shell line you sent.
The time-limited run prints three lines and exits with 124.
nova-run-42 is still active 15 seconds after systemd-run returned, and the journal says it started as agent.
Your check-then-start line exits 0 both times, and list-units shows one nova-run-43 unit.
After systemctl stop, is-active prints inactive for nova-run-43.
You removed the pretend VM (docker rm -f sandbox) and stopped LocalStack (docker stop localstack).

solution.text:
LINE='systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-43 || systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-43 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run run-43'

docker exec sandbox sh -c "$LINE"; echo "exit $?"
# Running as unit: nova-run-43.service; invocation ID: ...
# exit 0
docker exec sandbox sh -c "$LINE"; echo "exit $?"
# exit 0   (the unit is active, so nothing new starts)

docker exec sandbox systemctl list-units 'nova-*' --no-pager
docker exec sandbox systemctl stop nova-run-43
docker exec sandbox systemctl is-active nova-run-43
# inactive

lab.fix: A teammate shortened the start line to only systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-44 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run run-44, because "the check is noise". Send it twice. The second time, systemd refuses with "Failed to start transient service unit: Unit nova-run-44.service was already loaded" and exit code 1. In the platform, that second command is a retry after an orchestrator restart, and a failed command makes the activity decide the harness could not start, so a perfectly healthy run would be treated as broken. Put the check back, and explain why the refusal by itself is not enough.
explain: Why can the orchestrator send commands to a VM whose security group accepts no incoming connections?
Why does the SSM command start a systemd unit instead of running the harness itself?
Why must the start command be safe to send twice, and how does the check-then-start line make it safe?
lab.done: A time-limited run dies at its limit while nova-run-42 lives on in systemd, your start line is safe to send twice, and the pretend VM and LocalStack are gone.

check.q: The sandbox security group has no ingress rules. How does a command from the orchestrator reach the VM?

options.text: Through a temporary SSH key that SSM installs
options.why: No key is installed and no port is opened. Run Command does not use SSH at all.

options.text: The SSM agent on the VM connects out to Systems Manager and receives the commands waiting for it
options.why: The connection starts on the VM, through the private endpoints, so nothing ever needs to connect in.

options.text: AWS opens port 22 for the length of the command
options.why: Security groups never change by themselves. The VM stays closed the whole time.

check.q: Why does the start command use systemd-run instead of running nova-worker directly?

options.text: Because systemd-run makes the harness faster
options.why: Speed is the same. The difference is who owns the process when the command ends.

options.text: Because only systemd can run a program as the agent user
options.why: Other tools can change the user too. The reason is the command's time limit.

options.text: Because an SSM command is stopped at its timeout, at most 48 hours, and a run has no time limit
options.why: The command ends in a second, and systemd keeps the harness alive for as long as the work needs, with its logs in the journal.

check.q: An orchestrator worker restarts, and Temporal retries the activity that starts the harness. The harness is already running on the VM. What should the retried command do?

options.text: Find the unit active and do nothing, so the retry joins the running harness
options.why: That is what the systemctl is-active check gives you: the command is safe to send twice, and the work is never started twice.

options.text: Stop the running harness and start a fresh one
options.why: That would destroy work on every retry. Retries must never destroy progress.

options.text: Start a second harness in a new unit, so one of them survives
options.why: Two harnesses on one checkout would fight over the same files and branch.

p: The orchestrator's workInSandbox activity, which routines also use, starts the harness over SSM with AWS-RunShellScript and systemd-run as the agent user, in a unit named after the run. After that it follows the harness through the broker's heartbeats every 30 seconds; a retry finds the unit running and attaches to it. The claim activity writes the task, the capability and the gateway token to /run/nova/ over SSM as well, which is why the command history is on the threat model.

The nightly image test uses the same path: a small script sends one command to a fresh VM, waits for its result and fails the build if it fails. The orchestrator's role may send AWS-RunShellScript only to instances tagged ai-agents:managed=true.

tickets.why: workInSandbox: start nova-worker with systemd-run over SSM, follow heartbeats, re-attach on retry.
Writes the task, capability and run token to /run/nova/ over SSM after claiming a VM.
The orchestrator's role: SendCommand with AWS-RunShellScript, only on tagged instances.
The nightly smoke test runs its checks on a fresh VM through one SSM command.
The threat model that lists the SSM command history as a known soft spot.

words.plain: The AWS Systems Manager program on a VM that connects out and runs the commands waiting for it.
Sending a job (a document plus parameters) to VMs with SendCommand, then reading each machine's result.
How long an SSM shell command may run before SSM stops it: one hour by default, 48 hours at most.
One thing systemd manages, such as a service it starts, watches and logs.
A unit created on the spot with systemd-run, without a file written in advance.

review.q: Write the one-line start command for run-50 from memory, and say what each half does.
review.a: systemctl is-active --quiet nova-run-50 || systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-run-50 /usr/local/bin/nova-worker run /run/nova/task.json. The first half checks whether the run's unit is already active; the second half starts it as the agent user only if not.

review.q: A teammate wants to pass a GitHub token to the VM in an SSM command "just for one test". What do you answer?
review.a: Command parameters are stored in the account's SSM history, readable by anyone who can list commands. Real secrets never go into commands; GitHub access stays in the broker.

review.q: Explain where the comparison "SSM is SSH without port 22" stops.
review.a: There is no live terminal: you send a job, the agent runs it, and you read the result later, and the job has a time limit.

remember: The VM calls out for its commands, so nothing has to call in, and the command only starts a systemd unit, because a command has a deadline and a run has none.
